Django's own tree holds one server, the one runserver starts: WSGI only, built on the standard library's `wsgiref.simple_server`, and by its docstring not for production (`django/core/servers/basehttp.py`).
If the setting is `None`, it serves what `get_wsgi_application` returns (`django/core/servers/basehttp.py:get_internal_wsgi_application`).
Django's `pyproject.toml` names three dependencies beside Python 3.12 or newer: asgiref 3.12.1 or newer, sqlparse 0.5.0 or newer, and tzdata on Windows only (`django:pyproject.toml`).

The first two are imported at the top of the modules that use them: asgiref before `django.setup` runs, since the module a server or manage.py starts from imports the signals, whose dispatcher imports asgiref (`django/dispatch/dispatcher.py`), and sqlparse with a database backend's operations, when the backend is loaded.

`BaseHandler.adapt_method_mode` fits each layer of the middleware chain to its caller: a synchronous layer called by an asynchronous one is wrapped in `sync_to_async`, which runs it on a thread, and the reverse in `async_to_sync` (`django/core/handlers/base.py:BaseHandler.adapt_method_mode`).
The centre of the chain fits the view to the chain in the same way, and `Signal.send` calls its asynchronous receivers through `async_to_sync` (`django/dispatch/dispatcher.py:Signal.send`).
`QuerySet.aget` is `QuerySet.get` run by `sync_to_async`, and `Model.asave` and `BaseCache.aget` are made the same way (`django/db/models/query.py:QuerySet.aget`).

It holds the active language, the active time zone, the current URLconf and each connection handler's connections, though the databases' stay in their thread (`asgiref:asgiref/local.py:Local`, `django/utils/connection.py:BaseConnectionHandler.__init__`).

DEP 9, Andrew Godwin's Django Enhancement Proposal for an async-capable Django, made asgiref an install-time dependency: `sync_to_async`, `async_to_sync` and `Local` were already written there, in an official Django project (`deps:accepted/0009-async.rst`).
So the databases' connections are kept in a thread-critical `Local` (`django/db/utils.py:ConnectionHandler.thread_critical`).

The introspection of SQLite and of MySQL parses SQL the database gives back, such as a table's `"CREATE TABLE"` statement or a check constraint's clause, to find constraints, their columns and, on SQLite, each column's collation (`django/db/backends/sqlite3/introspection.py:DatabaseIntrospection._parse_table_constraints`, `django/db/backends/mysql/introspection.py:DatabaseIntrospection._parse_constraint_columns`).

Its time zones are the standard library's `zoneinfo` (`django/utils/timezone.py:get_default_timezone`), which reads the system's database of time zones and, where there is none, as on Windows, the tzdata package's.

The module is imported when the connection of its alias is first asked for (`django/db/utils.py:ConnectionHandler.create_connection`), so a missing driver raises `ImproperlyConfigured` then, naming the driver, in the backends for PostgreSQL, MySQL and Oracle.
PostgreSQL: `psycopg`, or `psycopg2` where it is absent (`django/db/backends/postgresql/base.py:Database`).
MySQL and MariaDB: `MySQLdb`, from the mysqlclient package (`django/db/backends/mysql/base.py:Database`).
Oracle: `oracledb` (`django/db/backends/oracle/base.py:Database`).
SQLite: the standard library's `sqlite3` (`django/db/backends/sqlite3/base.py:Database`), so a new project, whose settings name SQLite, needs no driver installed.

`DatabaseErrorWrapper` raises each error again as Django's class of the same name, so that code above the backend catches one `IntegrityError` whatever the driver (`django/db/utils.py:DatabaseErrorWrapper.__exit__`).

PyYAML's absence is caught when the serializers are first registered, and the YAML serializer becomes a stand-in that raises when called (`django/core/serializers/__init__.py:register_serializer`).
In a `try` at a module's top, the import can set a flag: without docutils, the admin's documentation pages say so (`django/contrib/admindocs/views.py:BaseAdminDocsView.dispatch`).
